items.new: There is some sweet mystery about this sea — no one knows quite what — whose gently awesome stirrings seem to speak of some hidden soul beneath — like those fabled heavings of the Ephesian sod over the buried Evangelist St. John. And it is fitting that over these sea-pastures, wide-rolling watery prairies and Potters' Fields of all four continents, the waves should rise and fall, and ebb and flow unceasingly; for here millions of mixed shades and shadows, drowned dreams, sleepwalkings, reveries — all that we call lives and souls — lie dreaming, dreaming, still; tossing like sleepers in their beds; the ever-rolling waves made so only by their restlessness.

This done, pole, iron and rope — like the Three Fates — remained inseparable, and Ahab moodily stalked away with the weapon, the sound of his ivory leg and the sound of the hickory pole both ringing hollowly along every plank. But before he entered his cabin, a light, unnatural, half-bantering, yet most piteous sound was heard. Oh, Pip! Your wretched laugh, your idle but unresting eye, all your strange mummery blended, not without meaning, with the black tragedy of the melancholy ship, and mocked it!

items.reason: 'and at the last one pause' is a reread trap (reads as 'the last one'); 'men yet may roll' keeps archaic 'yet'. Minimal grammar fixes only.
items.new: Oh, grassy glades! Oh, ever-vernal endless landscapes in the soul; in you, though long parched by the dead drought of the earthy life, in you, men may still roll like young horses in new morning clover; and for some few fleeting moments feel the cool dew of the life immortal on them. Would to God these blessed calms would last. But the mingled, mingling threads of life are woven by warp and woof: calms crossed by storms, a storm for every calm. There is no steady unretracing progress in this life; we do not advance through fixed gradations and pause at the last one — through infancy's unconscious spell, boyhood's thoughtless faith, adolescence's doubt (the common doom), then skepticism, then disbelief, resting at last in manhood's pondering repose of If. But once gone through, we trace the round again; and are infants, boys, and men, and Ifs eternally. Where lies the final harbor, from which we unmoor no more? In what rapt ether sails the world, of which the weariest will never weary? Where is the foundling's father hidden? Our souls are like those orphans whose unwedded mothers die in bearing them: the secret of our paternity lies in their grave, and we must go there to learn it.

items.reason: 'Meanwhile, while his whole attention was absorbed' doubles while, awkward aloud.
items.new: Now, in that Japanese sea, the days in summer are floods of brilliance. That unblinkingly vivid Japanese sun seems the blazing focus of the glassy ocean's immeasurable burning-glass. The sky looks lacquered; there are no clouds; the horizon floats; and this nakedness of unrelieved radiance is like the unbearable splendors of God's throne. It was well that Ahab's quadrant, the instrument for measuring the sun's height, was fitted with colored glasses through which to sight that solar fire. So, swinging his seated body to the roll of the ship, and with his astrological-looking instrument to his eye, he held that posture for some moments to catch the exact instant when the sun should reach its precise meridian. Meanwhile, as his whole attention was absorbed, the Parsee was kneeling beneath him on the ship's deck, and with his face thrown up like Ahab's, was eyeing the same sun with him; only his eyelids half hooded his eyes, and his wild face was subdued to an earthly passionlessness. At length the desired observation was taken; and with his pencil on his ivory leg, Ahab soon calculated what his latitude must be at that precise instant. Then, falling into a moment's reverie, he looked up again toward the sun and murmured to himself: "You sea-mark! You high and mighty Pilot! You tell me truly where I am now — but can you cast the least hint of where I shall be? Or can you tell where some other thing besides me is living this moment? Where is Moby Dick? This instant you must be eyeing him. These eyes of mine look into the very eye that is even now beholding him; aye, and into the eye that is even now equally beholding the objects on the unknown, far side of you, you sun!"

items.reason: 'Level by nature to this earth's horizon are the glances of man's eyes' is inverted and needs a reread.
items.new: Then, gazing at his quadrant and handling one after another its many cabalistic contrivances, he pondered again, and muttered: "Foolish toy! Babies' plaything of haughty Admirals, and Commodores, and Captains; the world brags of you, of your cunning and might; but what, after all, can you do, except tell the poor, pitiful point where you yourself happen to be on this wide planet, and the hand that holds you — no! not one jot more! You cannot tell where one drop of water or one grain of sand will be tomorrow noon; and yet with your impotence you insult the sun! Science! Curse you, you vain toy; and cursed be all the things that cast man's eyes aloft to that heaven whose live vividness only scorches him, as these old eyes are even now scorched with your light, O sun! By nature, the glances of man's eyes are level with this earth's horizon; not shot from the crown of his head, as if God had meant him to gaze on his firmament. Curse you, you quadrant!" dashing it to the deck. "No longer will I guide my earthly way by you; the level ship's compass, and the level dead-reckoning, by log and by line — it is these that shall guide me, and show me my place on the sea. Aye," stepping down from the boat to the deck, "thus I trample on you, you paltry thing that feebly points on high; thus I split and destroy you!"
